item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports aligning item content with collaborative representations, but the retrieved papers provide limited direct evidence for lightweight text encoders trained entirely from scratch. [DenseRec (RecSys workshop 2025)](https://earl-workshop.github.io/pdf/recsys2025-workshops_paper_167.pdf) jointly learns a projection from pretrained content embeddings into the recommendation space, using stochastic replacement of ID embeddings during training. It highlights a relevant failure mode: semantic similarity alone cannot distinguish items with different user appeal or contextual relevance. Its experiments use SASRec and pretrained embeddings, so results do not directly establish effectiveness under the required BERT4Rec setting. [Q-BERT4Rec (2025; revised 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02474) combines semantic feature injection, residual quantization and varied masking; its multimodal, multistage design is substantially heavier than the requested approach.\n\nA plausible adaptation—not an established result from these papers—is a small, randomly initialized token-embedding encoder with mean pooling or a shallow CNN over public titles and descriptions. Jointly optimize this encoder, item-ID embeddings and the existing BERT4Rec backbone through masked-item prediction, optionally adding a modest item-level text–ID alignment loss. Shared tokens could transfer training signal to sparse items, while ID residuals preserve fine item distinctions. Keep one jointly trained network and one scoring function per category; mask the entire target representation, including its text, to prevent leakage. Test whether text actually improves macro validation HR@10 rather than assuming semantic alignment helps. Product text may encode compatibility claims, but cannot establish a user's equipment ownership or current needs."}
